In 913 AD, a Balkan army camped outside the walls of Constantinople and the Byzantine Emperor came out to negotiate a crown for its ruler.

That ruler's grandfather had been a pagan steppe nomad.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ The Bulgars weren't from the Balkans at all. They were a Turkic-speaking horse people from the Pontic steppe who crossed the Danube around 680 AD and beat back the Byzantine army sent to remove them.

2/ Byzantium did something almost unheard of: it signed a treaty in 681 recognizing this new state and agreed to pay it tribute. A frontier camp became a country with a border Constantinople acknowledged in writing.

3/ The Bulgars were always a minority ruling a larger Slavic population. Within a couple of centuries they'd linguistically dissolved into their own subjects — modern Bulgarian is a Slavic language — while the state kept the conquerors' name.

4/ Khan Boris I converted to Christianity in 864, but not out of piety. Byzantium had just beaten him using a famine and a run of earthquakes as cover. Baptism was the peace price, and a tool to fuse Bulgars and Slavs into one people.
5/ It wasn't popular. In 866, fifty-two boyar families revolted against the new religion and were crushed. Old steppe aristocracies rarely go quietly into a new faith.

6/ Boris's real masterstroke: he gave refuge to the exiled disciples of Cyril and Methodius, whose students in his capital refined a script that became the Cyrillic alphabet — still used by roughly a quarter billion people today.
